_comment: How this language's phrases hold together, for lib/chunker.py. Optional, like every file of this name.
_why: English puts the adjective before its noun (the big house) and its prepositions before it (in the house).

function_words._comment: The closed classes, which a dictionary is the wrong authority on: Wiktionary files `man` under an interjection and a pronoun as well as a noun, and `not` under a conjunction, and the reading it listed first used to decide the cut. A word under two headings is read in its place (lib/chunker.py _in_context): `that man` is a determiner, `that he` a conjunction, `that is` a pronoun; `in the house` a preposition, `came in and` a particle of the verb. The order of the headings is the order a word under several of them is tried in when its neighbours say nothing. The wh-words are conjunctions here because they open the clause they introduce (docs/lang/en.md: `asked him | what he was waiting for`).

_particles: The prepositions that are also the particle of a phrasal verb (docs/lang/en.md: `give up`, `take the coat off`). One with no noun after it -- before a verb, a conjunction or the end -- is read as the verb's, and stays with it: `given up | counting the days`. Any other preposition before a verb is a preposition still: `accused him | of having stolen it`.
_ties: Prepositions that tie a noun to the noun or adjective before them rather than opening a phrase of their own: `a pound of apples`, `bigger than me`. The seam before them leans toward joining, where before any other preposition it is a cut.
_enclitics: What English writes into the word before it. The token `I'd` is a pronoun to what precedes it and an auxiliary to what follows, so `I'd like` holds together as `he would like` does.
